summary: Teach the K-Pg mass extinction (~66 Mya, ending the non-avian dinosaurs) for ages 9-11 as evidence-to-conclusion detective work rather than a told story. Learners assemble converging independent clues (a worldwide iridium-rich clay layer, shocked quartz and tektites, the buried ~180 km Chicxulub crater, and iridium found inside the crater by drilling) and then reason through the causal chain: impact -> dust/soot/sulfate aerosols block sunlight -> impact winter -> photosynthesis crashes -> plants die -> herbivores starve -> carnivores starve -> ecosystem collapse. Core nature-of-science goals: the strength of a case comes from multiple independent lines agreeing; a genuine rival hypothesis (Deccan Traps volcanism) persists and evidence, not authority, decides; and birds are surviving dinosaurs, so extinction was near-total, not total.
misconceptions: 'The asteroid killed the dinosaurs on impact' — most died from the global aftermath (impact winter, food-chain collapse), not the blast itself.
'All dinosaurs died' — avian dinosaurs (birds) survived; dinosaurs are not entirely extinct.
'Dinosaurs and early humans overlapped' — ~66 My separate the extinction from humans.
'One clue proved it' — the case rests on multiple independent evidence lines, not a single discovery.
'Science has closed the book' — a genuine minority hypothesis (Deccan volcanism) persists; debate continues.

activities.title: Assemble the case file: what killed the dinosaurs?
steps: Open a 'case file' and visit several boundary sites on a world map (e.g. Italy, Denmark, New Zealand, and a land site such as Hell Creek in Montana, USA); at each, examine the rock column and find the thin clay band at the boundary. At land sites like Hell Creek, non-avian dinosaur fossils are found below the band and none above it; at old sea-floor sites like Italy and Denmark, many kinds of tiny sea fossils found below the band disappear above it.

Run an iridium measurement at each site and record where the reading spikes — notice the spike lands at the clay layer at each site you visit, and that similar spikes have been found at the boundary at many sites around the world.

State in your own words why iridium at this layer points to space: iridium is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids, so a worldwide layer of it suggests material that fell from the sky everywhere at once.

Examine two more independent clues from a large impact: shocked quartz, which forms under the intense shock pressure of an impact, and tektites, which are droplets of rock melted and flung out by the impact's heat and energy — both are products of one large impact rather than both being pressure-formed.
Reveal the buried ~180 km Chicxulub crater in the Yucatan on a geophysics view, and check that its age matches the clay layer.
Drill a core into the crater and find the same iridium signature inside it; draw or describe the link that ties the crater to the global layer.
Write down which clues are independent and explain why two or more clues that agree make a stronger case than any single clue alone.
activities.insight: A scientific conclusion is built from converging independent evidence: chemistry (iridium), geology (shocked quartz, tektites, crater), and matching ages all point the same way, and drilling into the crater closed the link between the local crater and the global layer.

activities.title: Run the aftermath: trace the causal chain
steps: Starting from a thriving Cretaceous scene, release the dust and soot from the impact and reduce incoming sunlight (for example, by lowering a sunlight slider) to model an 'impact winter'.
Observe and describe, in order, what happens as sunlight drops: plants dim and die, then plant-eaters (herbivores) starve, then meat-eaters (carnivores) that fed on them starve.
Explain in your own words why plant-eaters are affected before meat-eaters, using the idea that energy enters a food chain through plants/photosynthesis.
Write the full causal chain as a sequence: impact -> dust/soot/aerosols -> sunlight blocked -> photosynthesis crashes -> plants die -> herbivores die -> carnivores die -> ecosystem collapse.
State clearly that worldwide extinction came from these after-effects, not from the blast crushing or burning dinosaurs everywhere, and note that the impact itself mainly devastated the local area.
Add a note that birds are surviving dinosaurs, so the extinction was near-total, not total.
activities.insight: Mass extinction was caused by ecosystem collapse — blocked sunlight shutting down the food supply across the whole planet — rather than by the impact directly killing animals far from the crater; and survival of birds means dinosaurs are not entirely extinct.

activities.title: Weigh the rival hypothesis
steps: Compare two explanations for the extinction: the asteroid impact and Deccan Traps volcanism, considering what each can explain and whether both might have played a part.
List which pieces of evidence (worldwide iridium layer, shocked quartz, matching-age crater, iridium inside the crater) fit the impact explanation.
Discuss or write why the impact case grew stronger over decades as new evidence arrived, and why a minority of scientists still support the volcanism idea.

Conclude with a statement about how scientists decide between rival ideas — by how much evidence each explains, not by authority — and that scientific conclusions can be revised as evidence accumulates.
activities.insight: Scientific knowledge is based on empirical evidence and is provisional: competing hypotheses are judged by how well they explain the evidence, and a genuine rival idea can still have supporters while the main case strengthens.

activities.title: Check your understanding of the case
steps: Put the causal chain in the correct order: impact -> dust cloud -> less sunlight -> photosynthesis crashes -> plants die -> herbivores die -> carnivores die -> ecosystem collapse.

Sort clues into 'impact evidence' (e.g. worldwide iridium layer, shocked quartz, matching-age Chicxulub crater, iridium inside the crater) and items that are NOT impact evidence (e.g. an ordinary dinosaur fossil from older rock, a present-day volcanic rock, a river-worn pebble).
Answer why iridium is a clue (it is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids).

Answer the diagnostic question: 'An asteroid hit near Mexico ~66 Mya and most dinosaurs died. Did it kill them all just by crushing or burning them on impact? Explain how a strike in one place could wipe out dinosaurs all over the world.'

Respond to probes such as: since birds are living dinosaurs, is it right to say the asteroid killed ALL the dinosaurs? Why do plant-eaters die before meat-eaters? What evidence shows the effects reached the whole world? Was the K-Pg really the deadliest extinction ever?
activities.insight: Learners can state the age (~66 Mya), name the Chicxulub crater, cite the worldwide iridium layer, order the food-chain-collapse mechanism, and avoid the direct-killing, total-annihilation, and 'biggest-ever' misconceptions.

checkQuestion: About 66 million years ago an asteroid hit the Earth near Mexico and most dinosaurs died out. Did the asteroid kill all those dinosaurs just by crushing or burning them when it hit? Explain how a strike in one place could wipe out dinosaurs all over the world.
checkAnswer: No — the impact itself only devastated the local area. Worldwide extinction came from the after-effects: dust and soot thrown into the sky blocked sunlight for years, so plants died, plant-eaters starved, and then the meat-eaters that fed on them starved — the food chain collapsed globally. Evidence includes the worldwide iridium layer and the Chicxulub crater.
